Nelson collared lemmings (Dicrostonyx nelsoni) inhabit the Arctic tundra of western Alaska, where they exhibit a suite of life-history traits adapted to short, intense breeding seasons. Field studies indicate that neonates weigh approximately 5.3 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.3 grams] at birth, a modest mass typical of altricial microtine rodents. Like other arvicolines, Nelson's collared lemmings are capable of rapid population cycling, with females initiating reproductive activity at a relatively young age. Comparisons with the closely related Dicrostonyx groenlandicus suggest that at a core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], females attain sexual maturity approximately 40 days after birth [tp = approximately 40 days after birth]. This accelerated maturation schedule appears to be an adaptation to the brief Arctic growing season, allowing females to contribute to population growth within their first summer of life. Cohort-based analyses from the Seward Peninsula confirm that many females breed successfully in the season of their birth, underscoring the selective advantage of early reproductive onset in this high-latitude environment.

Gestation in Dicrostonyx nelsoni is relatively compressed, as is typical for small-bodied rodents occupying ephemeral, high-quality habitats. At the same normothermic body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], females carry their developing young for a gestation period of approximately 20 days [tg = approximately 20 days], a duration that aligns closely with estimates for the congeneric Dicrostonyx groenlandicus. This short gestation, combined with a post-partum oestrus that often occurs within hours of parturition, allows females to produce multiple litters in rapid succession during the ice-free months. The energetic demands of gestation are substantial for a mammal of this size, and lactating females must maintain high daily food intake to meet the metabolic costs of both milk production and thermoregulation in the cold tundra environment. Indeed, the ability to compress gestation while simultaneously investing in the next litter is a hallmark of arvicoline reproductive strategy.

Weaning represents a critical transition in the life cycle of Nelson's collared lemming, marking the shift from maternal dependence to independent foraging. Based on observations of captive colonies and extrapolating from data on Dicrostonyx groenlandicus, weaning occurs at approximately 16 days after birth [tx = approximately 16 days after birth] under the standard thermoneutral conditions of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. At this stage, the pups are fully furred and capable of ingesting solid vegetation, although they continue to nurse opportunistically for several more days. The swift attainment of nutritional independence is essential in the Arctic environment, where the brief summer window demands that young individuals accumulate sufficient fat reserves before the onset of winter. Weaned juveniles rapidly transition from a milk-based diet to one dominated by willow catkins, dwarf birch leaves, and various graminoids, mirroring the adult dietary niche within days of the transition.

Maximum longevity in Dicrostonyx nelsoni has been estimated at approximately 3.3 years [am = approximately 3.3 years] based on captive records for the closely related Dicrostonyx groenlandicus, a value recorded at a stable core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. In wild populations, however, few individuals survive more than one or two winters due to intense predation by jaegers, snowy owls, Arctic foxes, and stoats, combined with the energetic challenges of overwintering under deep snow. Some captive individuals have been documented to reach roughly 4 years [am = 4 years], consistent with the upper bound of small-bodied microtine rodents, though most free-living lemmings succumb to senescence or predation long before reaching this boundary. Longitudinal mark-recapture studies on the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta indicate that median adult survival rarely exceeds six months, making longevity a trait expressed predominantly under protected, captive conditions rather than in the wild.

Adult body size in Dicrostonyx nelsoni shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males typically attaining larger overall dimensions than females. The ultimate wet weight for adult females in this species reaches approximately 75 grams [Wwi = approximately 75 grams], while males can achieve a greater body mass, with field records reporting a maximum ultimate wet weight of about 86 grams [Wwi = about 86 grams]. This disparity in adult mass is thought to reflect sexual selection for larger male body size in the context of male-male competition for access to breeding territories during the short summer mating season. In terms of reproductive output, females produce litters averaging 3.4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.4 pups per litter], and can produce approximately 8 to 9 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 8 to 9 litters per year] under favorable conditions. This high annual fecundity underscores the capacity for rapid population growth that characterizes cyclic arvicoline populations, comparable to the reproductive output of other Dicrostonyx species such as Dicrostonyx groenlandicus.
